A1.notes.Q3: Admin data is standard; Absalon activity risks surveillance feel. Sensitive data must only be used if it demonstrably fixes bias or improves help for specific vulnerable groups.
A1.notes.Q4: Trust is paramount in advising. If I cannot explain why a student was flagged, they will not trust the offer of help or my assessment.
A1.notes.Q5: I would accept losing some total coverage if it ensures we don't systematically miss marginalized groups. Missing a student in crisis is worse than extra contact for others.
A1.notes.Q6: Email opens the door without pressure; meetings provide real support but must remain voluntary to avoid coercion feelings based on data flags.
A1.notes.Q7: Generic emails have low cost, so casting a wider net is okay. Personalized messages require high certainty; false positives here damage the advisor-student relationship significantly.
A1.Q8.1: I am concerned about 'self-fulfilling prophecies' where students flagged by the model feel stigmatized or labeled as failures before any human interaction occurs.

A2.notes.Q3: Performance and admin data are natural for advising; LMS tracking feels invasive unless accuracy gains are massive to justify trust erosion.
A2.notes.Q4: As advisors, we need clear reasons to tailor our approach during outreach; a 'black box' makes personalized support impossible and damages trust.
A2.notes.Q5: Missing vulnerable students is the greater harm. I would accept catching fewer total if it ensures marginalized groups are not systematically overlooked by the algorithm.
A2.notes.Q6: A generic email is a low-friction first step that preserves student autonomy; immediate contact allows for timely intervention before a crisis builds up.
A2.notes.Q7: Generic emails can safely reach many to ensure no one falls through the cracks, but personalized advice requires higher precision to avoid feeling intrusive or patronizing.
A2.Q8.1: The model must not create a feedback loop where flagged students are treated differently in grading or opportunities by faculty who see the flags inadvertently.

A3.notes.Q3: Course data is fine for early warning, but online tracking feels invasive. Sensitive data like disability/finance should only be used to ensure fair outreach, not just prediction accuracy.
A3.notes.Q4: As an advisor, I must explain *why* a student is flagged to build trust and avoid stigma. A 'black box' model would damage the advisory relationship.
A3.notes.Q5: Missing vulnerable students (false negatives) is worse than contacting someone who doesn't need help yet. I am willing to lose some total accuracy if it means we don't overlook specific groups.
A3.notes.Q6: Start with a low-stakes generic email to normalize support seeking. Contact should happen immediately when the model flags issues, as delays reduce effectiveness.
A3.notes.Q7: For generic info (low cost), cast a wide net. For personalized advisor time (high resource/stigma risk), be more selective to ensure the conversation is meaningful and respectful.
A3.Q8.1: Crucial that students know how data is used and have an opt-out mechanism for non-essential tracking to maintain trust in the university system.

S1.notes.Q3: My dropout experience makes me wary of data mining. I accept grades but fear platform tracking feels like surveillance.
S1.notes.Q4: As a student, I need to understand why I am flagged to trust the system and avoid feeling criminalized by an algorithm.
S1.notes.Q5: Missing students in support is worse than false alarms. Fairness means ensuring marginalized groups aren't systematically overlooked.
S1.notes.Q6: Early warning is key; waiting months misses the point. I prefer a non-intrusive email first, then an optional meeting.
S1.notes.Q7: A personalized message from an advisor is intrusive if unnecessary. Precision matters more when human contact is involved.
S1.Q8.1: The model must not influence grading or permanent records; it should be purely for support access only.

S2.notes.Q3: As an international student working part-time, I fear surveillance via Absalon data. My late logins often mean work shifts, not laziness. Sensitive data risks bias against non-EU students.
S2.notes.Q4: If the model flags me, I need to know why to trust it or contest it. 'Black box' decisions feel discriminatory and create anxiety rather than offering support.
S2.notes.Q5: Overall efficiency matters less if the system fails international students like me. We are more likely to be missed; we need equal chances of being identified for help, even at a cost.
S2.notes.Q6: I prefer a generic email first to see what support exists without immediate intrusion or mandatory meetings that I cannot attend during work hours.
S2.notes.Q7: For general info, cast a wide net is okay. But for personalized emails from advisors, accuracy matters; false positives waste their time and mine.
S2.Q8.1: The model must not assume that being an international student or working part-time automatically equals academic struggle without context. Cultural differences in study habits should be considered to avoid bias.

S3.notes.Q3: As a student with chronic health issues, I fear surveillance via Absalon data (click tracking). Disability info is crucial for fairness; using it proactively to tailor support should be acceptable regardless of overall accuracy gains.
S3.notes.Q4: Transparency is vital for trust, especially given my personal experience with health issues affecting studies. If I am flagged without a clear reason, it feels invasive and may deter me from seeking help.
S3.notes.Q5: Missing vulnerable students is the worst outcome. I would accept missing some overall cases if ensuring marginalized groups (like those with disabilities) are identified equally well prevents them from falling through cracks.
S3.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal and dismissive of real struggles. A personalized message or an invitation to a low-barrier meeting signals genuine care, which is essential for students hesitant to ask for help.
S3.notes.Q7: For generic emails, some noise is okay. However, personalized contact implies the university knows details about me; false positives here feel like a breach of privacy and could cause unnecessary stress.
S3.Q8.1: Students need control over opt-outs for specific data sources (like Absalon). Trust requires that students know their disability status won't be used to label them as 'at-risk' in ways that bias future hiring or academic standing.

S4.notes.Q3: As a student with ADHD who has dropped out, I fear 'surveillance'. Course data is okay if it flags me early. Disability info must be used to help, not label or exclude.
S4.notes.Q4: I need to know why I am flagged to trust the advice, especially with ADHD where patterns are complex. A 'black box' feels stigmatizing and unhelpful.
S4.notes.Q5: Missing students in vulnerable groups (like me) is worse than contacting some who don't need help. I'd accept losing ~5% total accuracy to ensure fairness.
S4.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored. A personalized message referencing my specific struggle (e.g., late submissions) feels supportive, not like a lecture.
S4.notes.Q7: For generic info, fewer contacts prevent spam fatigue. For personalized advice from an advisor, I want to ensure no one is missed if resources allow.
S4.Q8.1: The model must not be used for disciplinary action or negatively affect funding eligibility without human review and student consent.

S5.notes.Q3: As an international student, tracking course performance is fine and helpful. However, monitoring my digital activity on Absalon feels like constant surveillance. I fear this creates pressure rather than support.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged to trust the process. A 'black box' model that contacts me without a clear reason would feel confusing and intrusive, especially as an international student.
S5.notes.Q5: It is crucial the system finds students who need help in my group (international). Missing us due to bias is worse than contacting a few extra people unnecessarily.
S5.notes.Q6: A generic email allows me privacy and autonomy. I do not want to be 'chased' by advisors continuously or immediately, as this adds stress.
S5.notes.Q7: Since the intervention is low impact (email), I am slightly okay with some false positives. But if it involves personalized contact, we must be very precise to avoid unnecessary intrusion.
S5.Q8.1: The cultural difference in how feedback and support are given matters. International students might interpret a 'flag' differently than domestic ones; context is key.

S6.notes.Q3: As an international student who dropped out before, I fear profiling based on nationality or past struggles. Basic academic data is fine for early help, but tracking digital behavior feels invasive unless it significantly improves support.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged. If the system is a 'black box', it feels like surveillance rather than support. Transparency builds trust, especially for international students who might already feel uncertain.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is critical; the model must work equally well for everyone. I am willing to accept a small loss in total efficiency if it means international or first-gen students aren't missed more often than others.
S6.notes.Q6: I prefer a low-pressure generic email offering resources, with an option to request a meeting personally. A mandatory call or personalized message about my 'problems' might feel stigmatizing and intimidating.
S6.notes.Q7: For generic info emails, a balance is fine to reach people. However, for personalized messages or meetings from advisors, I prefer fewer contacts to avoid false alarms that make me anxious or feel watched.
S6.Q8.1: My previous dropout experience makes me sensitive to how systems perceive 'struggling'. If the model flags me based on my nationality language barrier rather than actual performance issues, it could reinforce negative self-perception.

S7.notes.Q3: As a student with dyslexia, I fear invasive tracking (Absalon) but welcome disability data to ensure support reaches those of us who need accommodations early.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged to trust the advice and avoid panic about privacy invasion.
S7.notes.Q5: Ensuring marginalized students like me are not missed is more important than overall efficiency or avoiding false positives for others.
S7.notes.Q6: A simple email reduces pressure; I prefer not to be called unexpectedly, but continuous monitoring feels too intrusive.
S7.notes.Q7: Personalized messages carry more weight and stigma risk than generic ones, so false positives must be minimized significantly there.
S7.Q8.1: The system should allow me to opt-out of data collection for this specific purpose if I feel it compromises my privacy without clear benefit.

S8.notes.Q3: Course data is necessary, but tracking Absalon activity feels like surveillance. As an immigrant who dropped out before, I fear nationality or financial status could bias the model against me unless it significantly improves help.
S8.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged, especially given my past dropout. A 'black box' feels discriminatory and would prevent me from trusting or accepting the support offered.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial for international students like me. I would accept missing a few total cases if it ensures marginalized groups aren't systematically overlooked by the algorithm.
S8.notes.Q6: A generic email is a low-pressure start; an optional meeting offers deeper support. Continuous outreach ensures I get help immediately when struggling, rather than waiting for yearly checks.
S8.notes.Q7: For generic info, balance is fine to avoid spam. For personalized messages from an advisor, precision matters more; I don't want a sensitive conversation initiated by false positives.
S8.Q8.1: The timing of intervention is critical. Contacting me too early might feel invasive or premature given my previous dropout history, while contacting me when stress levels are already high may be less effective.

S9.notes.Q3: As a student with health challenges, I fear invasive tracking. Grades are acceptable; Absalon data needs proof of help. Sensitive attributes like disability or nationality should generally be excluded to avoid stigma.
S9.notes.Q4: I need to know why I'm flagged. If the reason is opaque, I might not trust the offer of support or feel wrongly accused. Transparency is crucial for my engagement.
S9.notes.Q5: Missing students in need hurts more than unnecessary emails. As an international student, I worry models trained on domestic data miss us. Fairness must prioritize catching everyone.
S9.notes.Q6: An automated email is a gentle start that respects my privacy. A meeting should be optional, not mandatory. I have low energy due to health; unsolicited calls are overwhelming.
S9.notes.Q7: For generic emails, missing some is okay. But for personalized advice based on my specific struggles, I prefer fewer contacts to ensure accuracy and avoid false stigma.
S9.Q8.1: The model must not influence grading or future admission chances. Students need guarantees that being flagged won't create a permanent record against them.
